documents.title: New Patient Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
53 y/o man here to establish care. Previously seen at a primary care office in the area; that physician retired and he never found a replacement until now. Records requested, release signed last week.

No active complaints. Walks a fair amount at work, no exercise program beyond that. Sleeps fine. Mood good.

PMH: none. No surgeries.
Meds: none. No supplements.
Allergies: no known drug allergies.
FH: father has a bicuspid aortic valve, found when he was 50. Paternal uncle died at 64 of a ruptured ascending aortic aneurysm. Mother has high blood pressure.
SH: logistics coordinator at a warehouse, runs inbound scheduling and the floor crew. Lives alone in Williamsburg. Never smoked. A beer or two most weeks. No drugs.

Prevention per patient and prior office: colonoscopy around 2018, told normal. Tdap about five years ago. COVID vaccines x2 this spring at a pharmacy clinic. Never had shingles vaccine.

ROS: negative in detail.

Exam: vitals as charted. Well, pleasant. HEENT unremarkable. Neck supple, no adenopathy, thyroid not palpable. Heart regular rate and rhythm. Lungs clear bilaterally. Abdomen soft, nontender, no masses. No edema, pulses 2+ symmetric. Skin without concerning lesions. Neuro grossly nonfocal.

PHQ-2 0. AUDIT-C 2.

A/P: healthy 53 y/o establishing care.
- Fasting labs today: CBC, CMP, lipids, A1c. One-time hep C and HIV screens, he agrees.
- Shingrix #1 today, #2 in 2-6 months, nurse visit.
- Flu shot when this season's supply arrives in October.
- Colonoscopy: confirm date and result from records; if 2018 and normal, next due 2028.
- Tdap: confirm in records.
Return for physical in a year.

documents.title: Getting winded
documents.author: patient
documents.body: I wanted to ask about something. For maybe a year now if I walk up the hill by my house or the ramp at work I get out of breath and my chest gets tight and I have to stop for a minute. Then it goes away. Doesn't happen sitting around. I figured it was getting older but it's not getting better. Should I come in?

documents.title: RN triage: exertional chest tightness
documents.author: RN
documents.body:
Called pt re portal message. Chest tightness and SOB only with uphill walking/inclines, about 1 year, resolves with a minute of rest. None at rest, none waking him at night. No syncope. No fever, cough, leg swelling. Never smoker.

documents.title: Office Visit: Exertional Chest Tightness
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: getting short of breath and tight in the chest going uphill.

HPI: 55M, generally healthy, no meds. Over roughly the past year he has had to stop partway up inclines (the hill on his street, the loading ramp at work) because he gets winded and his chest feels tight. Settles after a minute standing still. Nothing at rest or at night. No fainting. Has not tried to push through it. No palpitations. No cough, no leg swelling.
No known coronary disease, no diabetes. Never smoker. Alcohol unchanged, occasional.
FH relevant here: father with a bicuspid aortic valve (found at 50); paternal uncle died of a ruptured ascending aortic aneurysm at 64; mother with hypertension.
Meds: none. Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: BP 128/78, HR 78, RR 14, rest as charted. Comfortable at rest.
Neck: carotid upstrokes symmetric.
Heart: regular. Harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur, loudest at the 2nd right intercostal space, transmits up into both carotids. Gets softer when he bears down (Valsalva). S2 is single. No gallop.
Lungs clear. Abdomen benign. No peripheral edema. Radial and pedal pulses intact.

ECG in office: sinus rhythm 76, normal intervals, no ST/T changes.

A/P:
1. Exertional dyspnea and chest tightness with a systolic ejection murmur at the base radiating to the carotids, single S2. This sounds like aortic stenosis, and with his father's bicuspid valve a bicuspid valve is the leading thought.
- Transthoracic echo, ordered today.
- CBC, BMP, lipids, TSH today.
- Hold off on strenuous exertion and heavy lifting until we have the echo. Walking on the flat is fine.
- Any chest pain at rest, fainting or near-fainting: 911.
- Will likely need cardiology depending on echo. Will call him with results.

documents.title: Lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Your blood work from yesterday is normal, including blood count and thyroid, so no anemia or thyroid issue explaining the breathlessness. The echo is the important test. The scheduler will call you with a date.

reports.text:
Indication: systolic murmur, exertional dyspnea. Technically adequate study, sinus rhythm.
Left ventricle: normal size and wall thickness, normal wall motion. LVEF 60% (biplane).
Aortic valve: bicuspid, with fusion of the right and left coronary cusps. Mild leaflet calcification. Peak velocity 3.4 m/s, mean gradient 25 mmHg, aortic valve area 1.2 cm2 by continuity. No aortic regurgitation.
Mitral, tricuspid and pulmonic valves: structurally normal, no significant regurgitation.
Aorta: root 3.6 cm at the sinuses, ascending aorta 3.7 cm.
Right ventricle normal size and function. Atria normal size. No pericardial effusion.
reports.conclusion: Bicuspid aortic valve (right-left cusp fusion) with moderate aortic stenosis. Normal LV size and function, LVEF 60%. Aortic root 3.6 cm, ascending aorta 3.7 cm.

orders.reason: Bicuspid aortic valve with moderate aortic stenosis, exertional symptoms

documents.title: Echo results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Called pt with echo. Bicuspid aortic valve (same thing as his father) with moderate narrowing (stenosis). Heart muscle pumps normally, EF 60%. Aorta measures normal size.
Explained this likely explains the uphill symptoms. Referral to cardiology placed today for evaluation and a surveillance plan.
Continue to avoid heavy straining/lifting for now. Return/911 precautions reviewed again: chest pain at rest, fainting.
He asked if it can be fixed. Told him valves like this sometimes need replacement eventually and cardiology will lay out timing. He will watch for their call.

documents.title: Cardiology Consultation
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Outside cardiology group: consultation letter
Date of visit: 07/01/2024
Re: Piotr Kelleher, DOB 12/27/1967

Dear Doctor,

Thank you for referring Mr. Kelleher, a 56-year-old warehouse logistics coordinator, whom you evaluated in April 2023 for exertional dyspnea and chest tightness, with an echocardiogram in May 2023 showing a bicuspid aortic valve with moderate aortic stenosis.

Over the last six months he describes steadily worsening fatigue and chest pain with exertion. Stairs now bring it on as well as inclines. On occasion he is briefly lightheaded after climbing stairs or walking uphill. No frank syncope. No orthopnea or edema.

Medications: none. Allergies: NKDA.
Family history: father with a bicuspid valve diagnosed at 50; a paternal uncle who died at 64 of a ruptured ascending aortic aneurysm; mother hypertensive.
Social: never smoker; 1-2 drinks weekly.

Exam: BP 122/76, pulse 74 and regular. Grade 3/6 crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to both carotids. Lungs clear. No edema.

Impression: bicuspid aortic valve with aortic stenosis, moderate by the 2023 study, now with progressive exertional symptoms.

Plan:
1. Repeat transthoracic echocardiogram, arranged for next week in our office, to restage the valve and reassess the aorta.
2. I will write again once the echo is read.
3. Continue to avoid heavy exertion. Seek care urgently for syncope or rest pain.

Sincerely,
Cardiology

reports.text:
Outside cardiology echo laboratory. Indication: aortic stenosis, follow-up. Sinus rhythm, good image quality.
LV: normal cavity size, normal wall thickness, normal regional and global function, LVEF 60%.
Aortic valve: bicuspid. Peak velocity 3.7 m/s, mean gradient 30 mmHg, AVA 1.1 cm2 (continuity). No aortic regurgitation.
Other valves without significant disease.
Aortic root 3.7 cm, ascending aorta 3.8 cm.
Normal RV. No pericardial effusion.
Compared with 05/2023: modest increase in velocity and gradient.
reports.conclusion: Bicuspid aortic valve with moderate aortic stenosis (Vmax 3.7 m/s, mean gradient 30 mmHg, AVA 1.1 cm2). LVEF 60%. Aortic root 3.7 cm, ascending aorta 3.8 cm.

documents.title: Cardiology follow-up letter
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Outside cardiology group: addendum
Re: Piotr Kelleher, DOB 12/27/1967

Dear Doctor,

Mr. Kelleher's echocardiogram of 07/09/2024 shows his bicuspid valve with stenosis that remains in the moderate range: peak velocity 3.7 m/s, mean gradient 30 mmHg, valve area 1.1 cm2, up slightly from last year. LV function is normal (EF 60%). Aortic root 3.7 cm and ascending aorta 3.8 cm.

We discussed the findings by phone. Plan is surveillance: clinic visit with repeat echo in 12 to 18 months, sooner if symptoms worsen, and he knows to call for syncope or chest pain at rest. No medication changes. He should keep avoiding heavy straining.

Thank you for involving us.
Cardiology

documents.title: Cardiology letter

Their plan is to check you and repeat the echo in a year to year and a half. Please make that appointment before you leave the building next time, and let either of us know right away if the symptoms get worse.

events.reason: Sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back

reports.text: Portable AP upright chest. Mediastinum is widened. Lungs clear. No pneumothorax. No pleural effusion.
Sinus tachycardia, 112 bpm. Nonspecific ST and T wave changes. No ST elevation and no pattern of acute infarction.
reports.conclusion: Sinus tachycardia with nonspecific ST-T changes, no infarct pattern.

reports.text: Limited bedside study in the emergency department. Mobile intimal flap in the proximal ascending aorta. Moderate pericardial effusion without right ventricular diastolic collapse. Calcified bicuspid aortic valve. LV systolic function grossly normal.
reports.conclusion: Intimal flap in the proximal ascending aorta with moderate pericardial effusion, no RV collapse.

reports.study: CT angiography chest, abdomen and pelvis
reports.text:
Technique: CT angiography of the chest, abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast.
Findings: Stanford type A aortic dissection. The intimal flap begins at the sinotubular junction and extends through the ascending aorta and arch into the descending thoracic aorta, terminating above the diaphragm. The flap extends into the origin of the left subclavian artery. Ascending aorta measures 4.6 cm. High-density pericardial fluid consistent with hemopericardium. The abdominal aorta is normal in caliber without dissection; celiac, superior mesenteric, renal and iliac arteries opacify normally. Lungs without consolidation. No acute abdominal or pelvic findings.
reports.conclusion: Acute Stanford type A aortic dissection from the sinotubular junction to the distal descending thoracic aorta, involving the left subclavian origin, with hemopericardium. Ascending aorta 4.6 cm. Abdominal aorta and branches spared.

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital emergency department
Date of service: 11/09/2025, arrival 14:22
Patient: Piotr Kelleher, 57M. Allergies: NKDA. Home meds: none.

HPI: Brought in by EMS. While lifting heavy boxes this afternoon he had abrupt onset of severe chest pain he calls tearing, going straight through to his back, constant since onset. History of bicuspid aortic valve (known since 2023) with aortic stenosis followed by cardiology. Family history of a paternal uncle who died of a ruptured ascending aortic aneurysm; father also has a bicuspid valve.

Exam: diaphoretic, in obvious distress. BP 95/50 right arm, 75/40 left arm. HR 112, RR 22, SpO2 96% RA, T 36.6. Heart sounds muffled, soft systolic murmur. Femoral pulses diminished bilaterally. Lungs clear.

ED course:
- ECG: sinus tachycardia, nonspecific ST/T changes, no infarct pattern.
- Portable CXR: widened mediastinum.
- Bedside echo: flap in proximal ascending aorta, moderate pericardial effusion without RV collapse.
- CTA chest/abdomen/pelvis: acute type A dissection, sinotubular junction to distal descending thoracic aorta, left subclavian involved, hemopericardium; abdominal aorta spared.
- Labs: CBC, BMP, coags and hs troponin unremarkable.
- Two large-bore IVs, type and cross. Analgesia. No pericardiocentesis. Permissive pressures given hypotension.
- Discussed with cardiac surgery at the tertiary center; accepted for emergency repair.

Impression: acute type A aortic dissection with hemopericardium.
Disposition: transferred by critical care transport at 17:40, condition critical.

reports.text: Post-operative study. Bioprosthetic aortic valve within root conduit, well seated. Mean gradient 10 mmHg. No paravalvular leak. LVEF 55%. Normal RV function. No pericardial effusion.
reports.conclusion: Well-functioning bioprosthetic aortic valve, mean gradient 10 mmHg, no paravalvular leak. LVEF 55%. No effusion.

reports.study: CT angiography chest, abdomen and pelvis
reports.text: Post-operative aortic root and hemiarch graft, intact, no leak or pseudoaneurysm. Residual dissection of the distal arch and descending thoracic aorta with patent false lumen. Descending thoracic aorta 3.4 cm. Abdominal aorta normal. No pleural effusion.
reports.conclusion: Intact root and hemiarch graft. Residual distal arch and descending thoracic dissection with patent false lumen, descending aorta 3.4 cm.

documents.title: Operative Report
documents.author: cardiac surgery
documents.body:
Tertiary center, cardiac surgery
Date of operation: 11/09/2025
Patient: Piotr Kelleher, 57M

Preoperative diagnosis: acute type A aortic dissection with hemopericardium; bicuspid aortic valve with aortic stenosis.
Postoperative diagnosis: same.
Procedure: emergency median sternotomy, evacuation of hemopericardium, aortic root replacement with a 25 mm bioprosthetic valved conduit with coronary button reimplantation (Bentall), hemiarch replacement under hypothermic circulatory arrest with antegrade cerebral perfusion.

Findings: tense hemopericardium, evacuated. Dissection from the sinotubular junction into the arch. Calcified bicuspid valve with stenosis, not suitable for preservation. Coronary ostia not involved.
Intraoperative TEE after repair: well-seated prosthesis, no paravalvular leak, preserved LV function.
Specimens: valve leaflets and aortic wall to pathology.
Condition: stable to ICU.

documents.title: Discharge Summary
documents.author: cardiac surgery
documents.body:
Tertiary center, cardiac surgery service
Admitted 11/09/2025 (transfer from regional hospital ED). Discharged 11/18/2025.

Diagnosis: acute type A aortic dissection with hemopericardium, bicuspid aortic valve with aortic stenosis.
Operation 11/09/2025: Bentall with 25 mm bioprosthetic valved conduit and hemiarch replacement.

Course: ICU three days. Extubated post-op day 1. Chest tubes out day 3. Transferred to the step-down unit, ambulating with PT, cleared for home.
Pathology: bicuspid valve with calcific degeneration; aortic wall with acute dissection.
Pre-discharge TTE 11/16: well-seated bioprosthesis, mean gradient 10 mmHg, no paravalvular leak, EF 55%, no effusion.
Pre-discharge CTA 11/17: graft intact; residual dissection of the distal arch and descending thoracic aorta, false lumen patent, descending aorta 3.4 cm.
Discharge Hgb 10.4.

Discharge medications (new):
- metoprolol succinate ER 50 mg daily
- aspirin 81 mg daily
- oxycodone 5 mg/acetaminophen 325 mg 1 tab every 6 h as needed, #20
Allergies: NKDA.

Instructions:
- Blood pressure goal under 120/80, check at home daily.
- Sternal precautions: nothing over 10 lb for 8 weeks; no driving for 4 weeks.
- Cardiac rehab once cleared at the surgical visit.
- Follow up: PCP within 1 week; CTA and cardiac surgery clinic at 1 month; cardiology in 6-8 weeks.

documents.title: Post-Hospital Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
TCM visit. Interactive contact 11/20 by RN.

57M with bicuspid aortic valve and moderate AS, here 6 days after discharge from the tertiary center. 11/9: lifting boxes, sudden tearing chest/back pain, regional ED found BP 95/50 R and 75/40 L, widened mediastinum, type A dissection with hemopericardium on CTA. Emergency Bentall with 25 mm bioprosthetic conduit and hemiarch the same night. Uneventful ICU course, discharged 11/18. Discharge summary, op note, path and imaging reviewed (graft intact, residual distal arch/descending dissection, descending 3.4 cm; TTE EF 55%, valve MG 10).

Since home: sore at the incision, now using oxycodone-APAP only at bedtime and thinks he can stop. Walking the length of the driveway and back a few times a day. Sleeping in a recliner. No fever, no wound drainage, no palpitations, no dyspnea at rest. Home BPs 108-118/66-74.

Meds: metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily, oxycodone-APAP prn (short course from hospital). NKDA.

Exam: BP 112/70, HR 62, weight 80.6 kg (82.5 at his September physical). Tired-appearing but comfortable. Sternotomy incision clean, dry, edges approximated, no erythema; sternum stable. Normal S1 and S2 with a soft systolic flow murmur. Lungs clear. No edema. Calves soft.

A/P:
1. S/p emergency repair of acute type A aortic dissection (Bentall with bioprosthetic AVR + hemiarch), residual distal dissection.
- BP at goal (<120/80) on metoprolol succinate 50. Continue, plus daily home log.
- Aspirin 81 daily for the bioprosthesis.
- Can stop the oxycodone when ready; acetaminophen alone after that.
- CBC, BMP today; expect post-op anemia.
- Cardiac rehab referral placed; start after the surgical visit clears him.
- Sternal precautions and no driving per surgery.
- CTA + cardiac surgery mid-December; cardiology after.
2. Work: out of work; will complete short-term disability forms when they arrive.
RTC ~3 months post-op, sooner prn.

documents.title: Lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Your kidney function and electrolytes are normal. Hemoglobin is 10.9, up from 10.4 at discharge, which is the expected recovery after surgery like yours. We'll recheck it in a couple of months, no iron needed now.

reports.text: One-month surveillance after aortic root and hemiarch replacement. Graft intact without leak or pseudoaneurysm. Residual dissection of the distal arch and descending thoracic aorta, false lumen patent, unchanged. Descending thoracic aorta 3.4 cm. Abdominal aorta normal. Sternotomy wires intact.
reports.conclusion: Stable residual dissection of the distal arch and descending thoracic aorta, descending aorta 3.4 cm. Intact graft.

documents.title: Cardiac Surgery Follow-up
documents.author: cardiac surgery
documents.body:
Tertiary center, cardiac surgery clinic
Visit 12/17/2025. Re: Piotr Kelleher, 5 weeks after Bentall (25 mm bioprosthetic conduit) and hemiarch for acute type A dissection.

Doing well. Off narcotics. Walking 20 minutes daily.
Sternum stable, incision healed. BP in clinic within goal on metoprolol.
CTA 12/16: graft intact; residual distal arch and descending dissection unchanged, descending 3.4 cm.

Plan: cleared to drive and to begin cardiac rehab. After 8 weeks he may lift progressively, but as a standing restriction no lifting over 40 lb and no straining or breath-holding with lifts. Surveillance CTA at 6 and 12 months after surgery. Cardiology to follow the valve and BP. We are glad to see him back as needed.

reports.text: Bioprosthetic aortic valve within root conduit. Mean gradient 11 mmHg. No paravalvular leak. LVEF 55-60%. Normal RV. No pericardial effusion.
reports.conclusion: Normally functioning bioprosthetic aortic valve, mean gradient 11 mmHg, no paravalvular leak. LVEF 55-60%.

documents.title: Cardiology Follow-up
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Outside cardiology group
Visit 01/06/2026. Re: Piotr Kelleher, DOB 12/27/1967

Dear Doctor,

Mr. Kelleher's planned December surveillance visit became this post-operative visit after his acute type A dissection on 11/09/2025, repaired with a Bentall (25 mm bioprosthetic valved conduit) and hemiarch replacement. Recovery is going well. He starts cardiac rehab this week.

BP 116/72. Healed sternotomy, soft systolic flow murmur.
Echo today: bioprosthesis functioning normally, mean gradient 11 mmHg, no paravalvular leak; LVEF 55-60%.

Plan:
- Continue metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, BP goal under 120/80.
- Continue aspirin 81 mg daily.
- Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures is indicated with his prosthetic valve; amoxicillin 2 g 30-60 minutes before. Please prescribe when he has dental work scheduled.
- CTA at 6 months (May) and 12 months (November) after surgery.
- Follow-up here after the May CTA.

Cardiology

documents.title: Office Visit: Post-op Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
3 months out from Bentall/hemiarch for type A dissection (11/9/25).

Feels close to normal. Rehab going well, halfway through, they say his numbers are good. No chest pain, no palpitations, no dyspnea walking. Sleeping in bed again. Home BP 105-118/64-76.
Seen by cardiac surgery 12/17 (cleared, standing 40 lb lifting limit) and cardiology 1/6 (valve working well, EF 55-60%, plan CTA May and November, dental prophylaxis when needed).
Wants to go back to work Monday 2/16. His job is mostly scheduling and coordinating; he can stay off the floor lifting.

Meds: metoprolol succinate 50 daily, aspirin 81 daily. NKDA.

Exam: BP 114/72, HR 60, wt 82.4 kg. Well. Sternotomy healed. S1 S2 normal, soft systolic flow murmur. Lungs clear. No edema.

A/P:
1. S/p type A dissection repair with bioprosthetic AVR. BP at goal. Continue meds. CBC today to recheck the post-op anemia.
2. Return to work 2/16 with the surgical restriction in writing: no lifting over 40 lb, no straining or breath-holding when lifting. Letter given.
3. Dental cleaning: let me know when booked and I'll send the amoxicillin.
RTC at annual physical in the fall, sooner prn.

documents.title: Return to work
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: To whom it may concern: Piotr Kelleher is under my care and may return to work on 02/16/2026. Per his surgical team he should not lift more than 40 lb and should avoid straining or breath-holding while lifting. This restriction is permanent. Please contact the office with questions.

documents.title: Cardiac rehab discharge summary
documents.author: cardiac rehabilitation
documents.body: Cardiac rehabilitation completed 03/31/2026: 36 of 36 sessions, no adverse events. Resting and exercise BP stayed within the team's limits on his current regimen. Improved exercise tolerance across the program. Discharged to a home walking program, 30-40 minutes most days, with continued avoidance of heavy lifting.
